TAU · GEOMETRY NOTE · 18 SEPTEMBER 2026

What shape is a dead region?

Use cells fitted to the event boundaries for local certification, and a shared azimuth coordinate to explore how those cells continue around the board. The measurements support substantial patches of dead positions; they do not yet establish one continuous tube.

1. The main wall changes which event stops the reply.

At ndpxhts24, the dominant change of stopping event is on reply arm (0,−). Foot 2 reaching the outer edge of a0 competes with foot 1 reaching the outer edge of r1. At the supplied seed their event angles are 63.692660° and 68.763598°, respectively. The first event stops the swing; the accepted limit is 63⅔°.

The equality of those event angles is the blue curve E01 below. Moving across it changes which event stops that arm. A positive throw margin can survive that change. Consequently, this curve is a boundary of a limit program, not automatically a boundary between dead and escaping positions.

Five requested rotation slices. Coordinates are offsets from the blue hub; t = R(θ−θ₀). The dashed and dotted squares have half-widths 1u and 0.4u. The star is the projected reference hub in every panel; only the middle rotation slice contains the actual seed. This is an arrangement of limit-related geometry, not a map claiming that every white point is dead.

The wider ±1.5u neighborhood also contains changes in starting line contact, an arm becoming too short to count, and further event-order candidates on (2,−). 2. Implement one local chart, with constraints from all three pivots.

For this seed, begin with pivot 0 because it owns the dominant boundary. Let e(a) = (cos a, sin a), and define:

P₀ = h + R e(θ)
u = P₀,y − P₀,y*                 tangential chart coordinate
v = H(P₀) / λ                   signed event-gap coordinate
t = R(θ − θ*)
λ = ‖∇H(P₀*)‖ ≈ 4.333deg/u      fixed scale at the seed

The seed has v ≈ 1.1703u. On this local patch, ∂H/∂Pₓ is nonzero. Given (u,v,t), set P₀,y = P₀,y* + u, solve H(P₀,x,P₀,y) = λv for P₀,x on the selected branch, then recover the hub:

θ = θ* + t/R
h = P₀ − R e(θ).

A rectangular parameter cell in (u,v,t) maps to a curved cell in the original pose space. Splitting at v = 0 follows E01 exactly. Bounds on H and its derivative must establish a unique inverse over the cell; switch charts where that derivative approaches zero. The linearized H above is a useful initializer, not the boundary used for acceptance.

The same event equalities in each pivot plane. The gray squares show how the requested hub slices translate into pivot coordinates. The blue curves stay fixed as θ changes. Orange curves are circle tangencies, including candidates that need not affect the current limit.

The other pivots are constraints on this same cell, not independent cells to union. From one chart, compute every foot exactly:

Pⱼ = P₀ + R[e(θ + 2πj/3) − e(θ)],   j = 1,2.

Cell = chart patch
       ∩ constraints pulled back from pivot 0
       ∩ constraints pulled back from pivot 1
       ∩ constraints pulled back from pivot 2
       ∩ start-state, rim, legality, and phase constraints.

Both directions share the geometric event locations for one pivot; their traversal order and reachable prefix differ. Store separate state-machine programs for the two directions. Intersect their constraints in the common physical pose cell. When another pivot's wall becomes dominant, re-chart the neighboring cell instead of trying to straighten every wall in one global coordinate system.

Initially, an oriented box aligned with ∇H is a reasonable inexpensive prototype. It reduces the staircase waste but still straddles a curved boundary. The local implicit chart above is the natural next step. Feeding it back through a loose hub-coordinate bounding box would surrender much of the benefit: evaluate event intervals in the pivot chart, or use certified constrained enclosures.

A separate chart for the long direction

For joint six-dimensional exploration, make shared azimuth an explicit coordinate. If the victim hub is away from the origin, use:

φ   = atan2(hᵥ,y, hᵥ,x)
r   = |hᵥ|
a   = Rot(−φ) hₐ
ψᵥ  = θᵥ − φ
ψₐ  = θₐ − φ

z = (φ, r, aₓ, aᵧ, ψᵥ, ψₐ)

hᵥ = Rot(φ)(r,0)        θᵥ = φ + ψᵥ
hₐ = Rot(φ)a            θₐ = φ + ψₐ.

Holding the other five coordinates fixed while changing φ rotates the whole configuration. This chart exposes the symmetry of the push calculation without requiring both hubs to have polar coordinates. Use an alternate chart near r = 0 and unwrapped angles inside each patch.

Continue cells along φ, splitting where the side-arc rules change. Reuse a transported attacking trajectory only after checking that its throwing time remains legal at the rotated position. The attacker's limits change too, including after a reply has pushed it. Push equivariance alone does not establish that every transported throw remains an available move.

3. Rotation independence is exact locally, with several necessary qualifications.

For a moving foot i and pivot p, define the fixed offset δᵢₚ = arg(e(2πi/3) − e(2πp/3)). If βₑ(P) is the absolute bearing about P of a geometric event, put gₑ(P) = βₑ(P) − δᵢₚ. On a fixed unwrapped branch:

sₑ(P,θ) = dir [gₑ(P) − θ] + 2πkₑ

sₑ = s𝒇  ⇔  gₑ(P) − g𝒇(P) = 2π dir (k𝒇 − kₑ).

The θ term cancels even when the two events belong to different moving feet, provided the distinct δ offsets are included. Thus A1 walls are planar curves extruded along θ in an arm's pivot chart. The cancellation survives all smooth branches; it does not remove event wrap, the initial state, or discrete sampling phase.

The offsets ±150° apply to pivot 0 only. In foot-index order the other offsets are δ₀₁ = −30°, δ₂₁ = −90°, δ₀₂ = +30°, and δ₁₂ = +90°. Computing them with the argument formula avoids a pivot-label error.

FamilyGeometry to implementQualification
A1 · event ordergₑ(P) − g𝒇(P) = constantTrack branch lifts, foot offsets, span gates, and the reachable event prefix.
A2 · circle tangency|P−C| = |D−ρ| or D+ρThe absolute value is essential. Handle P=C separately; when D=ρ the distance is constant over the entire swing.
A2 · ray tangencydistance(P, supporting line) = ρTwo parallel lines in the pivot plane, not circles. Retain the forward-ray and radial-band tests.
A3 · move legalityselected stop crosses 2°θ-dependent. Track event changes and initial invalid poses separately.
A4 · start state|fⱼ−C| = D, plus span raysCircle edges, relevant centreline-side bits in PR18, and ray segments gated by the radial band.
A5 · initial rim|fⱼ| = 67.167A circle in foot-j coordinates; all three feet constrain one pose.
A6 · substep phasesₑ(P,θ) = kΔ; Δ = 1/3°These retain θ dependence. Equal event gaps alone do not determine whether the events share a bin.

For two events, the condition |sₑ−s𝒇| < Δ is necessary for sharing a substep bin, but insufficient: a bin edge can lie between them. The actual test is floor(sₑ/Δ) = floor(s𝒇/Δ). Its edges depend on the absolute phase θ. This explains the thin gray bands and why an A1 split alone does not remove every refusal.

So the planar reduction covers A1, A2, and the underlying geometry of A4/A5, with the additional ray cases above. It does not turn the entire problem into one fixed two-dimensional arrangement. The maps between the three foot planes depend on θ. The combined object is a three-dimensional intersection of pulled-back planar constraints, with additional phase and legality surfaces.

A further simplification is available for same-foot A1 equalities: compute the fixed intersection point Q of the two target level curves. The pivot must satisfy |P−Q| = ρ. Thus E02–E04 can be represented by selected arcs of radius-ρ circles centered at intersections of the appropriate band-edge circles. Branch and direction tests select the relevant arcs. E01 involves two different feet and requires the more general phase-difference equation.

4. The evidence supports patches and a promising azimuth direction.

The axis scans and azimuth scans are valuable data. They distinguish a tiny bookkeeping radius from the much larger scales worth investigating. They do not determine the topology or thickness of the dead set.

Reported resultSupported conclusionNot established
78/78 axis samples pass at ndpxhts24 and 6dgqa1fd8The sampled lines reach ±1.5u in all six directions without a failed certificate.A solid six-dimensional box, or even uninterrupted intervals between samples. The center is repeated six times: these are 73 distinct poses.
ndpxhts24: 59% of the ±1u victim box accepted; ±0.4u accepted as one cellThe current method finds substantial accepted neighborhoods; fitting cells to E01 is worth testing.That all rejected volume is dead, or that box geometry explains every refusal.
l5807vazg: 60 of 72 sampled azimuths passThe configuration works at many widely separated orientations.300° of certified continuous arc, one connected tube, or a positive uniform tube radius.
6dgqa1fd8: all axis samples pass, yet mixed-coordinate grid poses escapeCoordinate interactions matter.A margin wall is absent throughout the surrounding box.

“A union of patches extended along shared azimuth and interrupted by changing move domains” is a useful working hypothesis. “A long thin tube” is a good search intuition, not a measured geometric classification yet. The physical length traced by one hub under rotation is also not the same metric as distance in the joint six-dimensional pose space.

Keep three boundaries separate: A changes the available replies or their event program; B changes whether a legal reply can be punished; C marks an inconclusive certificate. An A wall can lie entirely inside a dead patch. A C boundary says where computation stopped establishing the desired claim.

For the stated six-arm attack test, the relevant margin at a position is the infimum over legal replies of the best available attacking margin. A sampled escape supplies a negative witness. A positive finite collection of samples does not lower-bound that infimum without a justified bridge. Large changes between 0.4° samples likewise show steep or sensitive behavior; they do not by themselves establish a mathematical discontinuity at grazing. Switching the maximum between continuous arm-margin functions would preserve continuity.

6. The clockwise swing checks out, with two corrections to the drawing brief.

Blue and purple distinguish moving feet 1 and 2. Their paths lie on the same geometric circle; their clocks are separated by 60°. The pivot and hub circle are shown, together with the printed bands, corner discs, span rays, physical rim, and off-board threshold. The timeline carries event angles without crowding the board drawing. The full labeled event table is below.

The first foot enters a0 at 3.692660°, reaches its centerline at 4.885713°, and leaves its inner band edge at 6.074334°. The second foot repeats those geometric events 60° later. Its entry at 63.692660° is refused because the earlier crossing has been spent. The largest accepted step on the chosen 1/3° grid is 63.666667°.

There are 40 candidate event angles on this full turn. At this seed all pass the physical input gates; none is a span-ray or rim event. Indeed, |P| + ρ is less than 67.167u, so the entire moving-foot circle stays inside the off-board threshold. Both clocks see the same 20 geometric intersection points.

u = P − C, ψ = arg(u), φᵢ = θ + δᵢₚ
d(s)² = |u|² + ρ² + 2ρ|u| cos(φᵢ + dir·s − ψ)

c = (D² − |u|² − ρ²)/(2ρ|u|)
s = wrap₍₀,₂π₎ {dir [ψ ± acos(c) − φᵢ]}.

For the ray from C at bearing A, write v = −(uₓ sin A − uᵧ cos A)/ρ. Both roots are needed:

β₁ = A − asin(v)
β₂ = A + π + asin(v)             equivalent modulo 2π to A − π + asin(v)
s  = wrap {dir (β − φᵢ)}

Forward-ray condition: [u + ρ e(β)] · e(A) ≥ 0.
Arc-contact condition at the ray: ||u + ρ e(β)| − 40| < 0.81.

The PR emits roots for the complete supporting lines and supporting circles, then lets the rule evaluator ignore irrelevant inputs. That is a valid event-list superset; those roots should not all be drawn as physical arc encounters. No ray intersection occurs in this specific swing, so its picture cannot empirically test the ray branch; the branch formula follows from the line equation above.

Using the literal engine value R = 23.095 gives ρ = 40.0017134008u, not exactly 40. I retained that value throughout the computation. A mathematically exact equal-radius design would use R = 40/√3. A center pivot then carries the moving feet along r0 and through its four corners; it does not visit the four r1 corners at radius 53.3. With the rounded engine constant it rides within r0's contact band rather than exactly on its centerline.

The recorded witness family covers victim arm (1,+) over approximately 35.435°–43.000°, answered by attacker arm (2,+) with selected stops in 38.000°–50.296°, leading to accepted child traps. Those are ranges of a varying witness strategy, not a claim that every attacker stop in that interval works against every victim stop. Other reply portions are handled by immediate throws or the rest of the recorded certificate.

The useful depth statement is: the test sometimes needs a preparatory attacking move that leaves another dead position, rather than an immediate throw after the victim's reply. The log calls this plies=3; from the initial victim-to-move position, the recursive pattern can include victim reply → attacker setup → victim reply → attacker throw. The logger's ply label should be defined before using it as a conventional move count.

Do not read the negative statuses as a solved escape theorem. The inspected deadDeep implementation samples attacker stops, screens candidates, and caps full child-certificate attempts. Its status escape includes “no certified child found by this search.” One recorded example has a level-1 margin of only −0.15u and no candidate surviving the screen. That is weaker than a robust geometric escape witness. A missing certificate can also be a false negative for the searched horizon.

The eight unresolved deeper results all describe gaps whose endpoints are thrown or have witnesses, but which lack a common bridge at the substep scale. These are direct examples of kind-C limitations. The single positive example supports nested forcing at the method's empirical standard; it does not establish the volume of a deeper dead region, a count of human skill levels, or a prevalence estimate for Tau as a whole.

These logs contain complete positions and search outcomes, but not the mixed-coordinate cell samples mentioned for 6dgqa1fd8 and 0r8c3cohc. They strengthen the evidence discussion without locating those particular local margin contours. The companion data include a deduplicated result CSV, input hashes, and the extracted positive certificate.

8. The throw note contains useful lemmas, but not yet a valid throw theorem.

The subsequently supplied throw-theorem.md improves the proposed proof strategy by focusing on the actual rigid-body update. Its slide/spin formula is useful. However, several statements called “proved” need repair before the theorem can replace simulation. These are algebraic and logical gaps, not merely the absence of an interval implementation.

The update formula is sound; the signed deficit claim is not.

ℓ = r × n,  λ = s/(1 + ℓ²/I),  ε = λℓ/I,  I = 0.7R².
Δp · n = λ + sin(ε)ℓ − (1−cos ε)(r · n).
η = s − Δp · n = (ε−sin ε)ℓ + (1−cos ε)(r · n).

The last term can be negative. For r = (−R/√2, R/√2), n = (1,0), and s = 0.8u, the exact update gives η = −0.00337866u: the touched material point moves 0.80337866u along n. Thus the asserted 0 ≤ η is false. This does not destroy a one-sided lower bound; it changes the statement to an absolute-error bound:

|η| ≤ (1−cos|ε|)|r| + (ε²/6)(s−λ).
|ε| ≤ s/(2√I),   0.7s/1.7 ≤ λ ≤ s.

For |r| ≤ R and s ≤ 0.8u, these bounds give an error below 0.005u per solver update. Lemma 2's slide/spin bounds follow correctly from the update. But the movement of the old material contact point does not imply that the newly closest pair is exactly separated by D, or that the finite iterative solver leaves zero residual overlap.

Normal advance is not the exact separation request.

Even for two points initially separated by D = 2.88u, moving the attacking point 0.1u along the old normal and 0.2u tangentially produces a penetration of

2.88 − √[(2.88−0.1)² + 0.2²] = 0.09281504u, not 0.1u.

Finite rotation, changed normals, and migration of the closest points introduce additional differences. The formula δ·dir·J(pₐ−P)·n is a first-order advance. The equality s = a requires a proven error or inequality; the touched-point lemma does not supply it. The note's measured totals, 5.66u of advance and 5.59u of requested separation, already show that it is not an exact identity along that trajectory.

There is a useful tighter conditional cap bound. Every leg-axis point lies at horizontal distance at most √3R from the pivot. At a 0.4° attacker substep its displacement is at most 2√3R sin(0.2°) = 0.279264u. If the pair was initially nonpenetrating, its first separation request is therefore at most 0.279264/0.35 = 0.797897u. This keeps the 0.8u cap inactive for that first evaluation. It does not establish the same fact after intervening victim updates or residual penetration; those cases still need bounds.

Use the exact foot displacement for the barrier.

For the exposed foot F = c + Rf, let u = F/|F|. Convexity of the Euclidean norm gives an exact lower bound, with no radial Taylor remainder:

Δ|F| ≥ ΔF · u
      = λ(n · u) + R sin ε (Jf · u) + R(cos ε − 1)(f · u).

g = n · u + (ℓ/I)R(Jf · u)
Δ|F| ≥ λg − R[(1−cos|ε|)|f · u| + |ε−sin ε| |Jf · u|].

This is the bound to enclose over a state set. It concerns the exposed foot directly, rather than borrowing the old contact point's 0.005u error. The note's claim that the omitted radial errors stay below 10⁻⁴u from s ≤ 0.32u alone is false: at the spin-maximizing lever |ℓ| = √I, s = 0.32u, an initially radial exposed foot at radius 64u has linear gain 0.160000u but exact gain 0.15949324u. The difference is about 5.07×10⁻⁴u. The companion script evaluates this algebraic example.

A corrected sufficient theorem for the discrete engine

Let B₀ be a valid set of initial victim poses, and fix a legal attacker swing up to a chosen time. Construct validated enclosures Sₖ,ⱼ containing every state after attacker substep k and solver update j, including all branches that can occur. For each actual solver update, enclose the exact projected gain above by a lower bound bₖ,ⱼ. For a no-contact branch use zero; for an uncertain branch include the worst allowed outcome. If r₀⁻ is a lower bound on the initial exposed-foot radius, then

r₀⁻ + Σₖ,ⱼ bₖ,ⱼ > 67.167u
⇒ every initial state in B₀ throws that foot by the chosen time.

The proof is induction over the actual discrete updates followed by telescoping of the radial gains. This is a valid sufficient implication once the stated enclosures are established. The strict inequality matches the engine's off-board test. An interval evaluation of the exact norm increment could be sharper still.

The uploaded theorem's H1–H3 only constrain poses that touch; they do not require contact to occur or persist. As written they can be vacuous during a no-contact sweep, yet the theorem sums positive advances over all substeps. Contact begins only after several steps even in the supplied example. The corrected theorem counts actual bounded updates and therefore does not charge positive gain to a noncontact step.

It must also count every inner solver update, not one error allowance per attacker step. There can be up to ten passes, and the normal, lever, and closest segment can change between them. The reachable enclosure is generally a moving tube Sₖ,ⱼ, not just the initial ±1u box. H4's proposed total-slide budget depends on the unproved s≈a relationship; it cannot be used to close that argument without its own valid bound.

What remains to implement: enclose closest-segment candidates and feature switches; branch on contact, cap, horizontal-fraction floor, and any deep-crossing correction; propagate all accepted updates and their residual overlaps; verify the attack stays legal; and bound the radial gain through that state tube. A single tube pair can still switch among its twelve polyline segments. Logged nonactivation and “0.0000u” residuals are useful engineering evidence, not a universal zero-residual assertion.

The reported 127 valid perturbed poses all throwing, with substantial full-sweep margins, make this a promising target. They do not verify H1–H4 over a continuum. Nor would proofs of a few fixed throws alone certify an entire dead cell: every legal pushed victim reply must land in a covered throw domain, with all stop intervals covered. Closed-form victim limits specify that reply's angle domain; they do not enclose the attacker's displacement caused by the victim's push.

The practical next step is a validated discrete trace for one fixed throw, then a small initial-pose box, then coverage of a reply interval. That establishes the needed pieces without treating an unfinished theorem as an already available replacement for the empirical certificate.

9. A practical path to better cells

  1. Pin the rules and use event identities. Store the event tag, continuous branch, crossing state, and co-event bin. Use the descriptive nearest-line label only for display. Resolve the brief/code rule differences before comparing new region coverage to the existing percentages.
  2. Split on relevant boundaries. Enumerate circle levels, span roots, corner discs, start-state bits, and rim events. Retain the reachable prefix and predicates capable of changing it. Use the pivot-0 implicit chart around E01, with all other arm constraints pulled back into it.
  3. Prove the event program constant, or enclose all its possibilities. Interval signs can establish event order, root existence, span membership, and initial state. At close events, propagate every admissible ordering or bin occupancy through the tiny state machine. A grid agreeing on a stopping tag is useful evidence, but is not this proof.
  4. Handle phase clusters rather than splitting every grid line. Away from co-events, bound the selected event and floor its interval endpoints. Near A6, form a conservative union of the possible stopping domains. If it opens extra stops, the throw certificate must test those stops too. If the transition set cannot be bounded, retain an unresolved strip.
  5. Keep the throw certificate empirical. Sample and refine the full joint pose after each pushed reply. Use a common attacking arm to bridge where the existing standard permits it; preserve its contact-history checks and final engine checks. Measure distances after mapping back into physical pose space, or bound the chart Jacobian—one chart unit is not automatically one unit of the old metric.
  6. Continue along azimuth. Recompute both players' legal domains at each continuation cell. Cache transported physical trajectories where their validity is established. Refine between sampled orientations before claiming a continuous arc, and test a transverse neighborhood before claiming a tube.

The first benchmark should compare accepted volume, runtime, number of unresolved co-event strips, and actual escape witnesses in the same ±1u neighborhood. Success is increased useful coverage at the stated empirical standard; it is not merely a reduction in the number of box refusals.

10. What was checked, and what differs from the brief

Repository source: PR #18, pinned at e32f09d5be9600212c3d5294b70a3835f0517427. The relevant implementation is nn/forced-win.js, with rules extracted from the same revision's index.html. The companion bundle retrieves those same source files for reproduction.

CheckResult
Four supplied seeds × six armsAll 24 closed-form limits and descriptive signatures match the full engine ladder.
Twelve reproducible random poses in the ±1.5u victim cube × six armsAll 72 additional limits and signatures match; maximum limit discrepancy 3.34×10⁻¹⁵ radians.
Fixed pivot, rotation offsets up to ±3u/R, all three pivotsThe unwrapped event phase is invariant to 7.11×10⁻¹⁵ radians.
All 40 swing events substituted into their geometric level equationsMaximum distance residual 1.37×10⁻¹³u.
Local grids126,750 arm-limit evaluations for the main five slices; 76,050 for the rim example's three slices.

The primary A1 candidate catalog evaluates all pairs of the enumerated analytic event branches, retains physical input gates, and renders equalities before the nearby sampled stopping limit, with a two-substep allowance. It uses a 161×161 rendering grid per requested slice (0.01875u spacing). A2/A4/A5 geometry uses 241×241 rendering grids. This is a reproducible numerical atlas with analytic curve definitions, not an exhaustive interval decomposition of the full three-dimensional cube. Small unrendered features and features between the five slices have not been ruled out.

IssueSource-grounded correction
Crossing episodesThe pinned PR18 state machine can keep an episode charged while either moving foot is on a line; it is not simply one independent charge per foot entry. The pivot is excluded from sustaining this contact.
Starting on a lineBacking off the starting side is free; leaving on the opposite side is charged. A start-side bit can change at a centerline, in addition to the contact-band edges.
“Exact reach envelope”The interval routine encloses one tagged event. Selection of the stopping event over the cell is still checked by a pose grid. The complete domain claim is conditional until event selection is bounded as well.
“The box reaches the rim”An interval upper bound exceeding the rim can reflect overestimation; it is not by itself a witness that any feasible pose in the box is off board. The two l580 perturbations above are actual point witnesses.
Throw marginthrowMargin uses the maximum victim foot radius reached during the attacking sweep, not only the endpoint radius.
MetricThe brief specifies |dx|+|dy|+R|dθ|. PR18's dist6 uses hypot(dx,dy)+R|dθ| for each piece. The axis units coincide; multidimensional ball and slope claims require one consistent choice.
Grazing “discontinuities”The reported adjacent-sample jumps and changing attacker arm do not establish discontinuity of the underlying physical outcome map.
0.17u star radiusIt is not used here as a geometric scale or a certified lower bound on the dead set.
